lesson.title: Addition
lesson.body:
Add left to right. School taught you to start with the units, but in your head you want the big part of the answer first — it's what you'd say out loud, and you never have to reverse digits. Keep the first number whole and add the second one a place at a time:

586 + 247: 586 + 200 = 786, + 40 = 826, + 7 = 833.

For 4-digit numbers, add the top two digits as one chunk, then the last two: 4 735 + 2 869: 4 735 + 2 800 = 7 535, + 69 = 7 604.

Round and compensate. When an addend sits just under a round number, add the round number and take back the difference: 586 + 298 = 586 + 300 − 2 = 884. 47 + 39 = 47 + 40 − 1 = 86.

Three numbers: column sums. Add all the hundreds, all the tens, all the units, then combine: 347 + 586 + 219 → hundreds 10 (1 000), tens 13 (130), units 22 → 1 152.

Tips: say the running total to yourself after each step, and practise until the 2-digit + 1-digit steps (826 + 7) are automatic — that's where the time goes.

lesson.title: Subtraction
lesson.body:
Left to right. Take the subtrahend off a piece at a time, biggest piece first: 834 − 267: 834 − 200 = 634, − 60 = 574, − 7 = 567.

Compensation. If you're subtracting something just under a round number, subtract the round number and give the difference back: 724 − 298 = 724 − 300 + 2 = 426. 83 − 47 = 83 − 50 + 3 = 36.

Count up (the cashier's method). When the numbers are close or straddle a round number, find the gap by adding up from the smaller one: 612 − 487: 487 → 500 is 13, 500 → 612 is 112, so the answer is 125. For 4-digit numbers, hop to the next thousand: 7 352 − 2 868: 2 868 → 3 000 is 132, 3 000 → 7 352 is 4 352 → 4 484.

Complements from 1 000 / 10 000. "All from 9, the last from 10": 1 000 − 387 → 9−3, 9−8, 10−7 → 613. 10 000 − 4 736 → 5 264. This is how you make change, and it's the engine behind counting up (2 868 → 3 000 is 1 000 − 868 = 132).

Pick the method that makes every step a single easy move — with practice you'll see it instantly.

lesson.title: Multiplying by one digit
lesson.body:
Left-to-right partial products. Multiply the biggest place first and keep a running total — you'll hold one number in your head instead of a column of carries:

347 × 6: 300×6 = 1 800; 40×6 = 240 → 2 040; 7×6 = 42 → 2 082.

For 4-digit numbers, treat the last two digits as one chunk (you know 2-digit × 1-digit): 4 736 × 7: 28 000 → + 4 900 = 32 900 → + 36×7 = 252 → 33 152.

Near-round numbers: overshoot and subtract. 49 × 7 = 50×7 − 7 = 350 − 7 = 343. 398 × 6 = 400×6 − 2×6 = 2 400 − 12 = 2 388.

Decimals. Drop the decimal point, multiply the integers, then put back as many decimal places as the factor had: 4.7 × 8 → 47 × 8 = 376 → 37.6; 0.36 × 7 → 252 → 0.252. Always sanity-check the size: 4.7 × 8 ≈ 5 × 8 = 40.

The whole skill rests on instant single-digit times tables and quick additions like 2 040 + 42 — if a step feels slow, that's the thing to drill.

lesson.title: Multiplying 2-digit numbers
lesson.body:
There's no single best method — the skill is spotting which trick the numbers want. Check in this order:

  • Symmetric around a round number → difference of squares. 47 × 53 = (50 − 3)(50 + 3) = 2 500 − 9 = 2 491.
  • A nice factor → factor it. × 25 = × 100 ÷ 4: 48 × 25 = 12 × 100 = 1 200. Ends in 5 × even → halve & double: 35 × 48 = 70 × 24 = 1 680.
  • Close to a round number → overshoot and correct. 47 × 59 = 47 × 60 − 47 = 2 820 − 47 = 2 773. Near 100: 96 × 93 → 96 − 7 = 89 | 4 × 7 = 28 → 8 928.
  • Otherwise split one factor (the one with the smaller units digit): 47 × 63 = 47 × 60 + 47 × 3 = 2 820 + 141 = 2 961. Criss-cross (tens×tens, cross terms, units×units) is the same idea written as a column.

Specials: × 11: spread the digits and drop their sum in the middle, 47 × 11 → 4 (11) 7 → 517. Teen × teen: 13 × 17 → (13 + 7) × 10 + 3 × 7 = 221.

For 3-digit × 2-digit, split the 2-digit factor: 347 × 26 = 6 940 + 2 082 = 9 022. Memorize squares up to 30 or so — they make difference-of-squares instant.

lesson.title: Squaring
lesson.body:
Ending in 5: n5² = n × (n+1), followed by 25. 65² → 6 × 7 = 42 → 4 225. 345² → 34 × 35 = 1 190 → 119 025.

Near 50: (50 + d)² = (25 + d) hundreds + d². 47² → 25 − 3 = 22 → 2 200 + 9 = 2 209. 56² → 31 → 3 100 + 36 = 3 136.

Near 100: (100 + d)² = (100 + 2d) hundreds + d². 97² → 97 − 3 = 94 → 9 400 + 9 = 9 409. 104² → 108 → 10 800 + 16 = 10 816.

Anything else: go up and down by the same amount. Because a² = (a − d)(a + d) + d², pick d so one factor is round: 67² = 70 × 64 + 3² = 4 480 + 9 = 4 489. For 3-digit numbers, round to the nearest hundred: 304² = 300 × 308 + 16 = 92 416; 497² = 500 × 494 + 9 = 247 009; 347² = 300 × 394 + 47² = 118 200 + 2 209 = 120 409.

The 3-digit case needs a 2-digit square as a sub-step, so get the 2-digit squares fast first (and memorize 1²–25²). Hold the big product in your head while you work out d².

lesson.title: Division
lesson.body:
Chunking. Peel off a big, easy multiple of the divisor, then deal with what's left: 432 ÷ 6 → 420 ÷ 6 = 70, 12 ÷ 6 = 2 → 72. For 2-digit divisors, estimate the tens of the answer first: 1 035 ÷ 23 → 23 × 40 = 920, leaving 115 = 23 × 5 → 45.

Simplify first. Divide both numbers by a common factor — the answer doesn't change: 1 344 ÷ 48 = 672 ÷ 24 = 336 ÷ 12 = 28.

Friendly divisors: ÷ 5 = × 2 ÷ 10 (435 ÷ 5 = 870 ÷ 10 = 87); ÷ 25 = × 4 ÷ 100; ÷ 50 = × 2 ÷ 100.

Non-exact answers. Get the whole part by chunking, then turn the remainder into a decimal: 347 ÷ 23 → 23 × 15 = 345, remainder 2; 2/23 ≈ 0.087 → 15.1. Knowing reciprocals helps a lot here: 1/7 = 0.1429, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/9 = 0.111, 1/11 = 0.0909, 1/12 = 0.0833, 1/13 ≈ 0.0769, 1/17 ≈ 0.0588, 1/19 ≈ 0.0526 — so 5/17 ≈ 5 × 0.0588 = 0.294.

If the dividend is smaller than the divisor, shift it: 17 ÷ 43 = (170 ÷ 43) ÷ 10 ≈ 3.95 ÷ 10 = 0.395. Give 3 significant figures, rounded (not truncated).
